body:
India's economy before British political dominance

Before British rule, agriculture provided a livelihood to most Indians, but manufacturing and trade were also important. Indian artisans produced fine cotton and silk textiles, metal goods and other handicrafts. Indian cloth was valued in markets across Asia, Africa and Europe because of its quality, designs and skilled workmanship.

Surat in Gujarat was a major port connecting India with the Persian Gulf and Red Sea trade. Other important trading centres included Masulipatam on the Coromandel coast and Hooghly in Bengal. Merchants, bankers, transporters, spinners and weavers all participated in the textile trade.

Gujarat was also known for specialised textiles. Patola was woven in centres including Patan, Ahmedabad and Surat, while tie-dyed textiles associated with the bandanna tradition were produced in Gujarat and Rajasthan. In eastern India, Dhaka muslin was especially famous for its fine quality.

How colonial rule changed the economic relationship

European trading companies initially purchased Indian goods for sale abroad. As the English East India Company gained political power, however, it could influence both the production and purchase of these goods. A major turning point came in 1765, when the Company acquired the Diwani, or revenue-administration rights, of Bengal.

Earlier, the Company had generally needed to bring precious metals into India to finance its purchases. After acquiring revenue rights, it could use money collected from Indian taxpayers to purchase Indian goods for export. Consequently, goods could leave India without the Company having to introduce an equivalent amount of new purchasing power from Britain.

During the 19th century, British industrialisation brought a further change. Indian producers increasingly faced competition from machine-made British goods, while the colonial trading system encouraged the export of agricultural raw materials required by British industries.

Colonial economic transformation refers here to the change in India's economic structure under British rule: the decline of many traditional manufacturing activities, the growing importance of raw-material exports, and the transfer of part of India's resources and income abroad.

Three connected changes

  • Drain of wealth: Part of the income and resources generated in India was transferred abroad through colonial financial arrangements.
  • Deindustrialisation: Many traditional Indian craft industries lost markets and employment, while modern factory industries grew too slowly to replace them fully.
  • Commercialisation of agriculture: Cultivators increasingly produced crops for sale, including crops required by overseas industries and consumers.

These processes were closely related. The decline of handicrafts pushed some artisans towards agriculture. The demand for British industrial raw materials encouraged cash-crop cultivation. Revenue collections and overseas payments contributed to the drain of wealth.

Prelims focus

  • Surat was a major pre-colonial trading port on the Gujarat coast.
  • Dhaka was famous for fine muslin; Patan, Ahmedabad and Surat were associated with patola weaving.
  • In 1765, the East India Company acquired the Diwani of Bengal.
  • Colonial India increasingly exported raw materials and imported British manufactured goods.
  • Trap: India was not an exclusively agricultural economy before British rule; it also possessed important manufacturing and trading activities.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Ch. 3, Ruling the Countryside, pp. 26–27, and Ch. 6, Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners, pp. 65–70; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Ch. The Age of Industrialisation, section 3.1, pp. 113–114; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Ch. 1, Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence, sections 1.1–1.2, pp. 4–5.]

body:
What was the drain of wealth?

The drain of wealth was the transfer of economic resources and income from colonial India to Britain without a corresponding economic return to India. Early Indian nationalists argued that this transfer reduced the resources available for investment, employment and development within India.

The essential distinction is between payment for something India received and an outward transfer that did not provide an equivalent benefit. For example, an ordinary import of machinery involves payment abroad in exchange for machinery delivered to India. By contrast, a pension paid in Britain from Indian revenues to a retired colonial official transfers income abroad without providing a new good or service in return at the time of payment.

Dadabhai Naoroji and the Drain Theory

Dadabhai Naoroji (1825–1917) was a pioneering Indian nationalist and economic critic of British rule. He developed the Drain Theory, arguing that British administration and financial arrangements caused a continuing transfer of Indian wealth to Britain and contributed to Indian poverty.

Naoroji used economic figures, public accounts and arguments about trade and expenditure to challenge the claim that British rule was economically beneficial to India. He presented an early criticism of the drain in 1867 and developed his analysis in subsequent writings. His important work Poverty and Un-British Rule in India was published in 1901.

Naoroji came from a Parsi family with roots in Gujarat and was born in Bombay, now Mumbai. His connection with Gujarat is historically relevant, but his birthplace should not be confused with his family's ancestral connections.

How wealth was transferred abroad

Revenue-financed purchases

After the Company acquired revenue rights in Bengal in 1765, it could use Indian land revenue to purchase Indian products for export. This reduced its need to bring gold or silver from Britain to pay Indian producers. Indian resources were thus used to finance goods sent overseas.

Home Charges and other overseas payments

Home Charges was a term used for expenditure of the Government of India payable in Britain. Such payments included expenditure connected with the India Office in Britain, pensions, interest on debt and purchases of government stores and services abroad. Salaries and private profits remitted overseas also formed part of nationalist discussions of economic transfers.

Not all these payments were identical. Some represented payments for goods, services or earlier investments, while others were criticised as transfers without an equivalent benefit to India. The central argument of Drain Theory concerned the burden of outward payments and the resources thereby unavailable for domestic use.

Why an export surplus did not necessarily enrich India

An export surplus occurs when the value of goods exported exceeds the value of goods imported. Ordinarily, such a surplus creates a claim on payments from abroad. In colonial India, however, export earnings could be used to meet Home Charges and other overseas obligations rather than being received as gold, silver or funds available for domestic investment.

Therefore, India could export more goods than it imported and still experience an outward transfer of resources. Export surplus and drain of wealth are related but are not the same concept. A trade surplus describes the difference between exports and imports; the drain concerns the nature and consequences of the payments leaving India.

A distinction that prevents incorrect answers

Do not classify every payment to a foreign country as a drain. An import paid for at its value and an unrequited outward transfer are economically different transactions. The nationalist criticism focused on the colonial system's unequal financial obligations and their effects on Indian development.

Economic consequences

The drain reduced the resources potentially available for domestic investment in agriculture, industry and public services. The argument also connected India's poverty with its political subordination: important decisions about revenue, expenditure and overseas payments were made under colonial authority rather than by an accountable Indian government.

Prelims focus

  • Dadabhai Naoroji is most closely associated with the Drain Theory.
  • Naoroji lived from 1825 to 1917.
  • His work Poverty and Un-British Rule in India was published in 1901.
  • Home Charges included expenditure payable in Britain from Indian public finances.
  • An export surplus could coexist with a drain of wealth.
  • Trap: An export surplus is not itself proof that the exporting country received and retained an equivalent financial benefit.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Ch. 1, section 1.5, Foreign Trade, pp. 8–9; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Ch. 3, Ruling the Countryside, pp. 26–27; Reserve Bank of India, RBI Bulletin, Lord Meghnad Desai, Drains, Hoards and Foreigners, section The Drain: Its Size and Its Burden, 18 October 2004, consulted 20 November 2026; Azim Premji University, Dinyar Patel, Dadabhai Naoroji, sections on economic thought and the drain of wealth, consulted 20 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Dadabhai Naoroji: The Man Who Brought Statistics into Politics, 27 June 2017, consulted 20 November 2026; National Library of Ireland, catalogue entry for Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901 edition, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Indian exports could finance overseas obligations instead of producing equivalent domestic gains.

title: Drain of Wealth and Dadabhai Naoroji's Economic Critique

body:
The meaning of deindustrialisation

Deindustrialisation is a sustained decline in the importance of industrial activity, especially its contribution to employment and income. In colonial Indian history, the term is commonly used for the weakening of traditional handicrafts and manufacturing occupations.

Indian handicrafts did not disappear completely. The central problem was that many established occupations declined and large numbers of artisans lost earnings, while modern factories developed too slowly to provide employment to everyone affected.

Traditional handicrafts before industrial competition

Indian weavers produced fine cotton and silk fabrics for domestic and overseas markets. Skilled spinners prepared yarn, while weavers produced cloth and dyers and printers completed specialised designs. Textile production supported many households and related occupations.

Muslin from Dhaka, printed cotton textiles, intricate handwoven fabrics and specialised regional products were valued in international markets. Indian producers also benefited from networks of local merchants who arranged advances, transport and sales.

Major causes of decline

Company control over producers

After securing political power, the East India Company attempted to control textile purchases and weaken competition from other buyers. It appointed agents called gomasthas to supervise weavers, inspect cloth and collect supplies.

Weavers who accepted Company advances could be required to deliver their cloth to Company agents rather than sell it to another merchant offering a better price. This reduced their bargaining power. The system of advances was therefore not simply an ordinary loan arrangement; it could also be used to restrict a producer's freedom to choose a buyer.

Protective policies in Britain

British textile producers sought protection against Indian competition. In 1720, the British government enacted the Calico Act, restricting the use of printed cotton textiles in Britain. High duties also made Indian cotton textiles more difficult to sell in the British market.

As British machine-based production expanded, British manufacturers increasingly benefited from access to the Indian market. Indian producers did not generally receive equivalent protection against competing British factory goods.

Competition from machine-made cloth

Factories in Britain could produce large quantities of standard cotton cloth at relatively low cost. By the 1830s, British cotton cloth was entering Indian markets on a large scale.

Indian weavers now faced competition in both directions: their overseas markets contracted because of British competition and trade restrictions, while imported cloth reduced their sales within India.

Loss of established markets and occupations

The decline of courtly patronage and changes in trading networks also affected specialised crafts. Some weavers abandoned their occupations, migrated to towns or entered agricultural labour. The growing use of imported machine-spun yarn particularly harmed women who had earned a livelihood through hand spinning.

Why handloom production survived

Decline did not mean the complete disappearance of handlooms. Some types of coarse cloth and specialised fabrics continued to find buyers. Machine-made cloth could not easily reproduce every intricate woven border, sari design or regional textile tradition.

Handloom producers also adapted. In the 20th century, some adopted improvements such as the fly shuttle, which increased weaving productivity. Thus, individual crafts suffered severe losses even though parts of the handloom sector survived and later expanded production.

Hand spinning and handloom weaving are different activities. Imported machine-spun yarn sharply reduced demand for traditional hand spinning. Handloom weavers, however, could sometimes use machine-spun yarn and continue producing cloth.

Prelims focus

  • Deindustrialisation refers to industrial decline, not necessarily the disappearance of every industry.
  • Gomasthas were Company agents used to supervise weavers and collect textile supplies.
  • The Calico Act of 1720 restricted printed cotton textiles in Britain.
  • British machine-made cloth became a major competitor in Indian markets during the 19th century.
  • Imported machine-spun yarn particularly affected traditional spinners.
  • Trap: The East India Company's initial political expansion did not immediately end Indian textile exports; the later decline had several causes.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Ch. 6, Weavers, Iron Smelters and Factory Owners, pp. 66–73; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Ch. The Age of Industrialisation, sections 3.2–3.3 and 5.1, pp. 114–117 and 122–123; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 11, Ch. 2, Colonial Rule and Crafts, pp. 22–25; IGNOU, Colonial Economy, Unit 17, De-industrialization in India, sections 17.2 and 17.4, pp. 33–38, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Deindustrialisation: Why Traditional Indian Handicrafts Declined
